extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate CS students (CS103) learning mathematical proofwriting
extracted.subtask_description: A course handout describing seven concrete checklist items instructors will use when grading proofs and recommending what students should check in their own proofs. Focuses on style, logical scaffolding, variable scoping, and distinguishing proof/disproof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly articulate your start and end points
rubrics_metrics.description: When you’re writing a proof, ... it’s important to make sure that the reader has a clear sense of where it is that you’re going and how you’re going to arrive there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State explicitly what you assume and what you will prove (start and end points). Example: begin with 'Let A, B, and C be arbitrary sets where A ⊆ B and B ⊆ C. We will prove that A ⊆ C.' This orients the reader, forces precision while you work, and reduces hidden assumptions. Anti-pattern: dropping into manipulations without declaring context (the provided incorrect proof that mentions A, B, C and subset relations out of nowhere). Benefits: helps both reader comprehension and the author's problem-solving by forcing explicit articulation of assumptions and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each sentence 'load-bearing.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Every statement in a proof should advance your argument; specifically, each sentence should do one of three things: set up a goal, introduce a new variable, or combine preceding results into something new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check sentences against the three allowed roles: (1) Set up a goal (e.g., introduce a subgoal or auxiliary lemma), (2) Introduce a new variable (e.g., 'let x be an arbitrary bananafish' or instantiate an existential), (3) Combine preceding results into a derived mathematical consequence. If a sentence does none of these, it is likely unnecessary and should be removed. Use this as a cleanup pass after a first draft to remove tangents and redundant restatements. Examples/anti-patterns are given (restating definitions as filler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and properly introduce variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When you use a variable in a proof, explicitly state the name of the variable, what value it represents, and where it comes from; variables should be clearly typed as arbitrarily-chosen, existentially instantiated, or explicitly chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce variables with precise phrasing: 'Let n be an arbitrary even natural number' (arbitrary choice); 'Since n is even, there is some integer k such that n = 2k' (existential instantiation — k is not arbitrary); 'Let m = 2k^2' or 'Consider the set D = { x ∈ S | x ∉ f(x) }' (explicitly chosen/name-giving). Watch for placeholder variables (e.g., in set-builder notation) that do not denote values and must not be referenced outside their context. Avoid variable redefinition/confusion (e.g., saying 'any x' after you already introduced a specific arbitrary x). The handout uses programming analogies (C/C++/Java scoping and redeclaration errors) to illustrate improper reuse or ambiguous scope. Also warns about switching between placeholder and actual chosen-variable usage when moving from stating a goal to proving it; instead explicitly pick an arbitrary element before using it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make specific claims about specific variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer making claims about a named, specific (usually arbitrarily chosen) variable rather than broad, high-level claims about all objects of a type without explicit instantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of saying 'every element of A is an element of B' in the abstract, phrase it as 'Consider any element x ∈ A. Since A ⊆ B, we see that x ∈ B.' The handout emphasizes replacing vague universal-language with concrete arbitrary-variable proofs or proof-by-contradiction. High-level informal statements are considered too coarse and more error-prone; if you can't pin down specifics, that may indicate conceptual confusion. Examples include rewriting vague function injectivity statements into 'Consider any arbitrary x and y where x ≠ y. Then f(x) ≠ f(y).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't repeat definitions; use them instead
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid restating definitions in the abstract; assume the reader knows definitions and instead apply them concretely to the objects/variables in your proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeating a definition verbatim is often redundant and can violate other checklist rules (e.g., variable scoping or making non-specific claims). Prefer concise application: e.g., instead of long restatements like 'We know that x ... that every element of A is an element of B', simply write 'Since x ∈ A and A ⊆ B, we see that x ∈ B.' The handout gives multiple left-hand (bad) vs. right-hand (good) rewrites and explains that restating definitions makes proofs longer and noisier while introducing scoping/precision errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in complete sentences and complete paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be written in grammatically-correct English sentences and paragraph form (not as shorthand chains or bulleted lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'mugga mugga' test: read the proof aloud replacing mathematical content with 'mugga mugga'; if the resulting English is grammatical, the proof likely has appropriate sentence structure. Avoid using mathematical notation as the grammatical verb of a sentence (e.g., avoid sentences where '=' functions as the verb without an explicit subject/verb in English). Do not convert precise notation into clumsy English like 'n equals 2k'—instead introduce a subject/verb around the notation: 'Since n is even, we see that there is some integer k such that n = 2k.' Avoid shorthand symbols and board-style abbreviations (e.g., ∴, ∵) in written proofs. Also avoid structuring proofs as bullet/numbered fragment lists; use coherent paragraphs instead. Examples and bad/good rewrites are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between proofs and disproofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof argues that a theorem (true statement) holds; a disproof argues that a claim is false — label and structure them properly and do not confuse disproofs with proofs by contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate templates: 'Theorem: [statement to prove true] / Proof: [argument]' versus 'Claim: [statement to show false] / Disproof: [argument that the negation is true]'. Do not label a false statement as a 'Theorem' and then 'prove it is not true' using a 'Proof' header — that misleads readers. In a disproof you should show the negation is true (e.g., provide a counterexample), not assume the negation and derive a contradiction (which would be an incorrect use of proof-by-contradiction). The handout gives concrete incorrect vs. correct examples using A∩B = ∅ and shows how to present a disproof with explicit counterexample and correct labeling.
